items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: staying right there with Manuel Perez, Milford Piron, old man Gus Moret, and people like that, and you have to learn, otherwise you don't have nothing in your head if you can't learn with these fellas.

ctx.x: Mm-hmm. Well, you must have been an awful good soloist, changing from the rapids. There's so many things.

Well, the training that I had is responsible for it. Well, for instance, my daddy was a musician and in fact, most of my family were musicians. But staying right there with Manuel Perez, Milford Piron, old man Gus Moret, and people like that, and you have to learn, otherwise you don't have nothing in your head if you can't learn with these fellas. George Moret. Old man George Moret. Yeah.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1969-12-30
items.q: when George would take me on the jobs with him, I was only in the area of a lot of ten, twelve years old.

ctx.x: Back to New Orleans in the early days, what did George Moret sound like?

George Moret was a rough, well, I'll explain it in musical terms, a rough trumpet player. Very good musician. Old man George Moret lived about three or four blocks from my house in the family. Real close friends through my grandfather and my father. And George could read music and actually he came from the old school or the old professors too. But he was loud and rough, if I can recall real well. Because when I went to, when George would take me on the jobs with him, I was only in the area of a lot of ten, twelve…
Do you remember him as playing any jazz or remember him as a brass band? Well, yes.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: We lived right around the corner from Mr. Moret.

ctx.x: I remembered one time in the conversation your father mentioned George Moret, too.
Well, George Moret was one of the great trumpet players.
Yes. You know, if your father might have played with him or something?
